question.text: Does post-hoc probability calibration (Platt scaling or isotonic regression) improve the probability estimates of tree ensembles on tabular classification, and at what cost in discrimination?

data.claim: Probability calibration trees outperform both isotonic regression and Platt scaling in reducing root mean squared error when calibrating probability estimates from various base learners.
data.quote: We propose probability calibration trees, a modification of logistic model trees that identifies regions of the input space in which different probability calibration models are learned to improve performance. We compare probability calibration trees to two widely used calibration methods---isotonic regression and Platt scaling---and show that our method results in lower root mean squared error on average than both methods, for estimates produced by a variety of base learners.

citation.title: Classifier Calibration at Scale: An Empirical Study of Model-Agnostic Post-Hoc Methods

data.claim: Platt scaling has limited and inconsistent effectiveness in improving probability predictions across a range of models and datasets.
data.quote: Platt scaling exhibits weaker and less consistent effects.

citation.title: Calibration of Machine Learning Classifiers for Probability of Default Modelling

data.claim: Re-calibration using isotonic regression improves the Brier score loss for non-parametric models like Random Forests compared to Logistic Regression.
data.quote: Using re-calibration, the non-parametric models are able to outperform the Logistic Regression on Brier Score Loss.

data.claim: Random Forests are generally well-calibrated, and traditional calibration methods like isotonic regression provide only marginal improvements when data is limited.
data.quote: The Random Forest (RF) classifier is often claimed to be relatively well calibrated when compared with other machine learning methods. Moreover, the existing literature suggests that traditional calibration methods, such as isotonic regression, do not substantially enhance the calibration of RF probability estimates unless supplied with extensive calibration data sets, which can represent a significant obstacle in cases of limited data availability.

citation.title: ForeCal: Random Forest-based Calibration for DNNs

data.claim: The ForeCal method, a Random Forest-based calibration approach, improves calibration (as measured by ECE) without sacrificing discriminative performance (AUC).
data.quote: ForeCal outperforms existing methods in terms of Expected Calibration Error(ECE) with minimal impact on the discriminative power of the base DNN as measured by AUC.

citation.title: A Lightweight Calibration-Selection Policy After a Probe Fit for Selective Classification on OpenML Tabular Tasks

data.claim: While calibration improves negative log-likelihood (NLL), it does not guarantee improvement in abstention quality, and may even degrade performance on risk-coverage metrics.
data.quote: Within this benchmark, both tested calibrators improve mean NLL relative to raw predictions on average, yet calibration can also worsen mean AURC, so better probability fit does not imply better abstention behavior.

citation.title: Probability Calibration Using Platt Scaling in SVM Based Fake News Detectors

data.claim: Platt scaling, when used in ensemble models like SVMs, can provide meaningful improvements in confidence estimation, especially with limited data.
data.quote: The findings suggest that even simple ensemble techniques can provide meaningful improvements, particularly in settings where data and resources are limited.

citation.title: Benchmarking Lightweight Machine Learning Models for Epileptic Seizure Recognition: Accuracy, Calibration, and Robustness Analysis

data.claim: Gradient boosting methods, including Random Forests, perform well in terms of both accuracy and calibration, and are efficient alternatives to deep learning models.
data.quote: Notably, all gradient boosting methods substantially outperform Logistic Regression, indicating that nonlinear feature interactions are critical for this task. Compared with prior deep learning approaches on the same dataset, these lightweight models achieve competitive performance at a fraction of the computational cost.

citation.title: Uncertainty-Gated Dual-Branch Additive–Attention Network for Robust and Calibrated Tabular Classification Under Missingness

data.claim: The proposed model achieves strong performance in both discrimination (AUC, AUPRC) and calibration (Brier, ECE), showing that calibration can be maintained without significant loss in discrimination.
data.quote: The model is also supported by sparsity, stability, and Brier-based calibration regularization. This allows it to balance expressive interaction modeling with transparency and robustness under incomplete data. DA2-Net achieves or shares the best result in all 16 AUC blocks, 13 of 16 AUPRC blocks, 10 of 16 Brier blocks, and 7 of 16 ECE blocks.

data.description: The evidence does not directly compare the impact of Platt scaling and isotonic regression on tree ensembles (e.g., Random Forests, Gradient Boosting) in terms of both calibration improvement and discrimination loss in a unified, controlled setting. While E1 shows probability calibration trees outperform both Platt scaling and isotonic regression in RMSE, and E2 notes Platt scaling's inconsistent effectiveness, there is no direct evaluation of how these methods affect discrimination (e.g., AUC) in tabular classification tasks with tree ensembles. This leaves a gap in understanding the trade-off between calibration and discrimination under different post-hoc methods.

The evidence on calibration performance (e.g., Brier score, ECE) and discrimination (e.g., AUC) is primarily limited to specific models or settings. For instance, E5 shows ForeCal (a Random Forest-based method) improves ECE without sacrificing AUC, but this is specific to a DNN base model and not directly applicable to tree ensembles as base learners. Similarly, E4 and E3 focus on Random Forests and Logistic Regression, without generalizing to other tree ensemble models like XGBoost or LightGBM. Thus, the generalizability of calibration gains across different tree ensemble variants remains untested.

There is a lack of empirical evidence on the cost of calibration in terms of risk-coverage or abstention quality, especially when applied to tree ensembles. E6 notes that while calibration improves NLL, it may worsen AURC (a risk-coverage metric), implying that better probability calibration does not necessarily lead to better decision-making under uncertainty. However, this is not evaluated in the context of tree ensembles or with any specific post-hoc method like Platt or isotonic regression.

The evidence does not systematically compare the computational cost, data requirements, or scalability of Platt scaling, isotonic regression, and probability calibration trees across different tabular datasets and tree ensemble configurations. For example, E4 suggests isotonic regression has limited gains with limited data, but no evidence evaluates the practical cost (e.g., training time, memory) of these methods when applied to large-scale tabular classification tasks.

data.independent_variable: type of post-hoc calibration method (Platt scaling vs. uncalibrated)
data.rationale: E1 shows Platt scaling is outperformed by probability calibration trees in RMSE (a Brier score-related metric), and E2 indicates Platt scaling has inconsistent effectiveness. This hypothesis directly tests whether Platt scaling improves calibration (positive) but at the expense of discrimination (negative), addressing G1 and G2 by providing a clear, falsifiable trade-off under a controlled setting.
data.statement: Post-hoc calibration using Platt scaling improves probability calibration (as measured by Brier score) in tree ensembles on tabular classification tasks, but at the cost of reduced discrimination (as measured by AUC) compared to uncalibrated models.

data.independent_variable: type of post-hoc calibration method (isotonic regression vs. uncalibrated)
data.rationale: E3 shows isotonic regression improves Brier score in Random Forests, and E4 notes that RF is already well-calibrated but that isotonic regression provides marginal gains with limited data. This hypothesis tests the feasibility of isotonic regression as a low-data-cost, non-degrading calibration method, addressing G1 (lack of unified evaluation), G2 (narrow scope), and G4 (data requirements and scalability).
data.statement: Isotonic regression improves calibration (measured by ECE) in tree ensembles without significantly degrading discrimination (measured by AUC) compared to uncalibrated models, especially when data is limited.

data.rationale: The hypothesis focuses on post-hoc calibration via Platt scaling's impact on Brier score (calibration) in tree ensembles. To test this under controlled conditions, we select three balanced, real-world tabular datasets (breast_cancer, digits_binary, wine_binary) that are representative of classification tasks with moderate to high dimensionality and class balance. The control condition uses uncalibrated gradient boosting (a strong tree ensemble model known for good discrimination), while the treatment applies Platt scaling to the same model to assess its effect on calibration. Brier score is the primary dependent variable as it directly measures probabilistic calibration. A paired Wilcoxon test is used because it is appropriate for non-normal, small-sample comparisons of paired Brier scores across the same model variants. Five-fold cross-validation ensures robustness, and three random seeds ensure reproducibility and variance estimation. Excluded datasets with class imbalance (e.g., breast_cancer_imb10, digits_binary_imb10) are omitted to avoid confounding the calibration-discrimination trade-off due to imbalance, as the hypothesis is about calibration in standard settings. This design directly addresses gaps G1 and G2 by isolating the effect of Platt scaling on calibration (Brier) while holding discrimination (AUC) as a secondary concern, though AUC is not included in the primary metrics here to focus on the hypothesis's core dependent variable.

The hypothesis focuses on isotonic regression's ability to improve calibration (ECE) without degrading discrimination (AUC) in tree ensembles under limited data. We select datasets with varying sizes and class balance (including imbalanced variants) to test generalizability. The control (random_forest) represents the uncalibrated baseline, while the treatment (random_forest+isotonic) applies isotonic regression as a post-hoc calibration. We use ECE as the primary metric (dependent variable) and AUC as a secondary metric to assess discrimination stability. Paired Wilcoxon test is appropriate for comparing ECE between calibrated and uncalibrated models, as it handles non-normality and small sample sizes. Five-fold cross-validation ensures robustness, and three random seeds ensure reproducibility and variance estimation. The inclusion of both balanced and imbalanced data (via _imb10 suffix) addresses the hypothesis's focus on limited data and data scarcity. Excluded datasets (e.g., wine_binary) are smaller and less representative of high-dimensional, real-world settings with limited data. Datasets like digits_binary have high dimensionality and are more relevant to limited-data challenges due to sparse feature space.

limitations: The study only evaluates Brier score as the primary metric and does not measure AUC to assess discrimination, thus failing to test the trade-off claimed in the hypothesis; the datasets are small and balanced, limiting generalizability; the effect sizes are small and negative, suggesting Platt scaling degrades calibration rather than improving it; the Holm-adjusted p-values for the primary metric are only significant in one dataset, and even there, the result is not robust across all datasets.
data.statement: The hypothesis is not supported at alpha = 0.05 (Holm-adjusted, primary metric) because the mean difference in Brier score between gradient boosting with Platt scaling and uncalibrated gradient boosting is negative across datasets: in digits_binary, the mean difference is -0.00235 (95% CI: [-0.00311, -0.00161], p_holm = 0.00055), indicating worse calibration, and in other datasets, the differences are non-significant (e.g., breast_cancer: p_holm = 1.0). The evidence does not show an improvement in Brier score, which contradicts the expected positive direction of the hypothesis.

data.issue: The hypothesis claims that Platt scaling improves calibration (as measured by Brier score) but reduces discrimination (AUC), with evidence from E1 and E2. However, E1 states that 'probability calibration trees outperform both Platt scaling and isotonic regression in RMSE', which implies that the best calibration is achieved by probability calibration trees, not Platt scaling. This contradicts the claim that Platt scaling improves calibration. Moreover, E2 notes 'inconsistent effectiveness' of Platt scaling, which does not support a consistent improvement in calibration. There is no direct evidence that Platt scaling increases Brier score or decreases AUC; the evidence only shows it is outperformed by other methods. Thus, the hypothesis is not grounded in the evidence and misrepresents the direction of effect.
data.message: Hypothesis H1 is not supported by the evidence; claims of improved calibration and reduced discrimination are not substantiated by E1 or E2.

data.issue: The hypothesis claims isotonic regression improves ECE without significantly degrading AUC, especially with limited data. Evidence E3 shows isotonic regression improves Brier score in Random Forests, which is related to ECE, but E4 notes that RF is already well-calibrated and isotonic regression provides 'marginal gains' with limited data. This does not establish a significant or consistent improvement in ECE nor demonstrate that AUC is not degraded. Furthermore, E4 and E3 are limited to Random Forests, and there is no evidence on AUC performance under isotonic regression in other tree ensembles. The claim of 'no significant degradation' of AUC is not supported by any data. The hypothesis also assumes generalizability beyond Random Forests to other tree ensembles without evidence.
data.message: Hypothesis H2 overreaches by inferring ECE improvement and AUC stability from marginal gains in Brier score and limited data settings; lacks direct AUC evidence and generalizability to other tree ensembles.

data.issue: The gap description correctly identifies a lack of unified, controlled comparison between Platt scaling and isotonic regression on tree ensembles in terms of both calibration and discrimination. However, the evidence cited (E1 and E2) do not contain any evaluation of AUC or discrimination under these methods. E1 compares RMSE (a Brier score-related metric) with probability calibration trees, not with uncalibrated models or with each other. Thus, the gap is acknowledged, but the cited evidence does not actually support the need for the gap or the claim that a unified evaluation is missing.
data.message: Gap G1 is acknowledged, but the evidence does not actually show the absence of a unified evaluation; the cited evidence is insufficient to establish the gap's validity.

data.issue: The gap claims that calibration and discrimination are limited to specific models (e.g., Random Forests, Logistic Regression) and that generalizability to XGBoost or LightGBM is untested. However, the evidence (E3, E4, E5) do not provide any data on other tree ensemble models. The gap is well-identified, but the evidence is not sufficient to support the claim that generalizability is untested—there is no empirical evidence to back this claim. The gap is valid in concept but not substantiated by the evidence.
data.message: Gap G2 is conceptually valid but not supported by evidence; no data on other tree ensembles is provided to confirm the lack of generalizability.

data.issue: The gap mentions a lack of evidence on cost in terms of risk-coverage or abstention quality. Evidence E6 notes that calibration may worsen AURC (a risk-coverage metric), but this is about calibration in general and not specifically for tree ensembles or post-hoc methods like Platt or isotonic regression. There is no data linking AURC changes to Platt or isotonic regression in tree ensembles. Thus, the claim of a lack of evidence is not supported by E6, which does not specify the context (model, method, dataset).
data.message: Gap G3 is not supported by evidence; E6's mention of AURC is general and does not establish a link to tree ensembles or specific post-hoc methods.

data.issue: The gap claims a lack of evidence on computational cost, data requirements, or scalability. Evidence E4 and E1 mention limited gains with limited data and performance of probability calibration trees, but neither discusses training time, memory, or scalability of Platt or isotonic regression on large tabular datasets. Thus, the claim of untested computational cost is not supported by the evidence. The gap is identified, but the evidence is insufficient to validate it.
data.message: Gap G4 is not supported by evidence; E4 and E1 do not address computational cost, scalability, or training time.
